question: Can a convert accept inheritance from her non-Muslim mother and leave her wealth to non-Muslim relatives?
asked: I am a new convert and the only Muslim in my family, with no husband or children yet, and I am writing my will. I was told that Muslims do not inherit from non-Muslims, nor do non-Muslims inherit from Muslims. My mother has put my name in her will: if she passes on, am I allowed to take that money? And since my only relatives are my non-Muslim blood relatives, can I leave money to them?
answer:
The answer to this question is actually very simple. This is a misunderstanding of Islamic law that unfortunately people sometimes say to new converts, and this is one of the problems of people without knowledge, when they just spread things without research, without proper knowledge. They will say, "Oh, Muslims don't inherit from non-Muslims; non-Muslims don't inherit from Muslims." Now, there is an element of truth here, but the way that it is understood and the way that it is said to a convert is also false. It shouldn't be said so generically.

This misunderstanding comes from a hadith in Sahih Bukhari; it's an authentic hadith. Our Prophet ﷺ said that the Muslim does not inherit from the kafir, and the kafir does not inherit from the Muslim. This is a very clear, very explicit hadith, and it is authentic; it is in Bukhari and Muslim. It's an explicit hadith that the Muslim does not inherit from the kafir and the kafir does not inherit from the Muslim.

What does it mean, though, "inherit"? You see, when it comes to inheritance, a whole class can be given on it, but simplistically we can divide the money into two broad categories. When a person dies, there is a portion of their inheritance that is dictated by the Shari'ah of Allah. There is a portion that goes in fractions according to the Qur'an, according to Surah An-Nisa, because Surah An-Nisa has all of the fractions of inheritance according to the rules of Islamic Shari'ah. So for example, according to those rules in the Qur'an, one-eighth goes to a wife in certain circumstances, one-sixth goes to a mother, one-third goes here, one-half goes there. So this is very explicit; every category has a certain fraction.

Therefore, if a person dies without any will in an Islamic land, there is no need for a will in that case, because all of the money will go in accordance with how Allah has dictated the shares of the inheritors. There is no need to write a will if you're living in a land where the laws are going to be in accordance with Islam and you don't want to make any changes or any modifications that Allah has allowed you to make, as we're going to come to in part two of this question.

This is the section where the Prophet's hadith applies: the Muslim does not inherit from the kafir; the kafir does not inherit from a Muslim. So if there is a convert living in a land of Islam and her mother is a non-Muslim lady, when she passes away, then the share she would otherwise have gotten, let's say one-sixth or one-half, the share that Allah has assigned, in this case that share would not be there. The shares that Allah has assigned in the Qur'an are between Muslim family members. That's the point here.

So let's say there are two brothers and a father. One of the brothers is not a Muslim, one of the brothers is a Muslim, and the father is a Muslim. When the father dies, the Shari'ah would say that the two brothers share half each, if there are no other relatives (this is very simplistic), half each. But because one is a Muslim and one is a non-Muslim, Islamic law then says that the non-Muslim in this case is not going to take that share. He is removed from the shares of Allah 'azza wa jall.

Now, what's left? If a person wants to give a portion of their inheritance to somebody who is not in the shares of Allah, they have up to one-third, 33.33%. Up to one-third of their wealth they can give to somebody who's not in the list that Allah has assigned.

So, a simple example: you have a cousin who helped you out when you were young. Let's just say that cousin helped finance your education, and now, alhamdulillah, you are wealthy. Now that cousin is elderly, and their children are not that well off. You say, "I want to help that cousin's family, because he helped me." Now, generally speaking, if you have immediate family and children and brothers and sisters, the cousin is not going to inherit. But you feel a sense that "I owe something to that family." So you can say 15%, 20%, 30%, 33.33%: one-third of my wealth I want to give to that family. Completely halal. **That one-third you may give to a Muslim or a non-Muslim; it doesn't matter.**

Therefore, if you have a person in your family who is not a Muslim, and you want to give some money to them in your will, at the time you pass on, or vice versa, you may write in your will up to one-third for that person, and the rest will then go to the shares assigned by Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. I hope that is clear. So you may write your parents or whoever you want in your will; no problem.

Now, you are saying that you don't have any Muslim family members, and that at this stage you don't have any children, you don't have a spouse, all of your family is non-Muslim, and also that they might leave things for you. So in this case, according to the fatwa from a number of fiqh councils, including the European Council, including the Fiqh Council of North America, including AMJA, in this particular case even the one-third does not apply to you. Why? Because we're not living in the land of Islam. So if you wish, you can write a full will where you assign "this goes here, this goes there," because you don't have any blood relatives.

If you were living in the land of Islam, then your shares would go to the treasury, the Islamic treasury. The shares that Allah had assigned would go to the Islamic treasury, and one-third would go to the people that you have assigned. But there is no Islamic treasury over here. So if you want to give some to the masjid, your local masjid, or give some to charities, that's fine. And if you decide, "You know what, I don't have any blood relatives other than these family members, and I'm going to leave all of my wealth to them," in these circumstances that we are in, in the Western world where we are a minority, we are allowed to increase the one-third share, as long as, in your case, as you said, you are the only Muslim, a convert. If you have Muslim family members who will inherit from you, then you cannot supersede the shares that Allah has given, and you must give them their share, and they will also take your share.

So, bottom line: **you may take whatever your mother has gifted you; no problem.** She is not bound by the Shari'ah, and she may write in her will, "My daughter should get this much," and that is yours to take. And you as well may write in your will however much you want to give to various family members, and you are completely free to choose whoever you wish, because once again, the shares that Allah has assigned do not apply in this particular case.

So for example, if you have multiple siblings, but for whatever reason you want to give to a few of them and not all of them, you have the right to do so in this case. Why? Because the Shari'ah does not apply in your case, because these siblings are not following Islam. Otherwise, if they were all Muslim, then you could not pick and choose, and all of them would have a share if you had no children.

So you may therefore take your mother's wealth if she passes on (I'm assuming that your father has already passed on, since you're only mentioning the mother), and you may as well leave your inheritance, however much you want, to your relatives. And Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala knows best.
